title: JEP 545 Moves ZGC Memory Preparation off the Startup Path in JDK 28
gist: JEP 545, integrated into JDK 28, moves ZGC heap memory acquisition and preparation off the startup path onto concurrent ZMemoryWorker threads and, on Linux 6.1+, upgrades 4 KB pages to 2 MB pages in the background. Combined with adaptive heap sizing from JEP 546 (still off by default), the JEP's case study shows a 38% startup drop and warmup falling from 80 to 10 seconds for Spring PetClinic on a 32 GB machine, ending the startup-versus-warmup tuning trade-off.

insights.claim: Before JDK 28, deploying ZGC forced a trade-off: a tiny -Xms gave fast startup but long warmup as memory was acquired incrementally, while a large -Xms with AlwaysPreTouch gave fast warmup but paid the whole cost before the first request.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Removing this trade-off improves Java's suitability for autoscaled and serverless workloads where cold start matters.
insights.locator: A team chasing fast startup set

insights.claim: According to JEP 545, starting a JVM with a 2 MB heap takes roughly a tenth of a second versus more than ten seconds with a 32 GB heap on current hardware.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Quantifies the cold-start cost large heaps impose on cloud Java deployments.
insights.locator: A team chasing fast startup set

insights.claim: ZGC's pause times do not grow with heap size but its collection frequency does, so a small heap triggers early and frequent collection cycles.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Explains why heap sizing has driven ZGC tuning costs.

insights.claim: JEP 545 introduces a ZMemoryWorker thread per heap partition that commits and uncommits memory concurrently and pre-touches memory and collapses small pages into large ones before application threads reach it.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Concurrent memory preparation shifts JVM startup cost off the critical path.
insights.locator: That work now happens in a new thread

insights.claim: JEP 545's memory preparation budget is fixed rather than adaptive: ZConcurrentWorkersCPUShare is 0.25, capping preparation at a quarter of available CPU.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Startup gains come with bounded CPU overhead that matters for CPU-constrained containers.
insights.locator: The budget is fixed rather than adaptive.

insights.claim: On Linux 6.1 and later, ZGC probes for MADV_COLLAPSE and upgrades 4 KB pages to 2 MB large pages in the background, so administrators no longer need to reserve large pages up front; identical behavior across operating systems is a non-goal, so Windows may not get it by default.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Java performance increasingly favors newer Linux kernels, encouraging infrastructure upgrades.

insights.claim: Services on Linux 6.1 or later running a modest ZGC heap get concurrent pre-touch and background large pages in JDK 28 without changing any flag, because memory heating is on by default.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Free performance upgrade for existing Java fleets on JDK 28 lowers compute cost.

themes.theme: Adaptive heap sizing dependency and results

insights.claim: The headline JEP 545 results depend on adaptive heap sizing from companion JEP 546, which remains off by default and must be enabled with -XX:+ZAdaptiveHeapSizing.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Default deployments will not see the full advertised gains without opt-in configuration.
insights.quote: The 2 MB initial heap behind the JEP's headline numbers comes from elsewhere: adaptive heap sizing, in the companion JEP 546, which still defaults to off.

insights.claim: With ZGC adaptive heap sizing in JDK 28, the JEP's case study shows a 38% drop in startup time and warmup falling from 80 seconds to 10 for Spring PetClinic on a 32 GB machine.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Large warmup reductions cut over-provisioning needs for Java services, reducing cloud spend.

insights.claim: ZGC adaptive heap sizing lowers minimum and initial heap to 2 MB and raises the max heap ceiling to 100% of physical memory, but the policy holds a reserve, preferring to leave a fifth of the machine free, fighting for a tenth and enforcing a twentieth.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Memory-elastic JVMs could improve container density and utilization.
insights.quote: That 100% ceiling reads worse than it behaves.
insights.locator: Services already running a modest heap

insights.claim: JEP 545 cautions that applications tuned around a larger initial heap may warm up more slowly and need re-tuning, and pairing UseLargePages with adaptive sizing and no -Xmx disables explicit large pages with a warning.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Migration to JDK 28 carries re-tuning costs for heavily tuned fleets.

insights.claim: The MADV_COLLAPSE retry loop in ZGC can spin indefinitely when EAGAIN persists, a case the code attributes to pinning through mlock or long-term DMA and treats as user error.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Edge-case operational risk for specialized workloads using pinned memory.

insights.claim: JDK 28 reaches Rampdown Phase One on December 3, 2026, with general availability scheduled for March 9, 2027, and future work targets better CPU sharing and leveraging ahead-of-time compilation from JEP 544.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Sets the timeline for when enterprises can adopt these startup improvements in production.
